turns.doctor_question: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I suppose I’m here because... for months now, the property manager and certain people in my building have been trying to pressure me out of my apartment. They’ve been using things like misdelivered mail. Which is interesting, really, because back when I was doing management analysis for a large logistics firm in the late nineties—I have my master's in operations, you see—we proved that routing errors are almost never just random accidents. They're systemic. We spent six months redesigning their entire distribution matrix. I had to fly to Chicago almost every week for that project. The deep-dish pizza there is incredibly overrated, honestly, I don't understand why people rave about it. It’s more of a heavy casserole than a pizza, and the tomato sauce is always too sweet. 

But yes, the mail, and... they also make these timed noises in the walls. Very precise. And there are these little comments from the neighbors when I walk down the hall. They want me out. And they can show me all the paperwork they want, or give me their little explanations, but it doesn't change the pattern I can clearly see. I analyze patterns for a living, Doctor. Just like that logistics firm. They tried to hide their inefficiencies in the quarterly reports, but the data is the data. Did I mention the misdelivered mail is mostly gardening catalogs? I don't even have a garden, I'm on the fourth floor...

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that the property manager and neighbors are conspiring to force them out using misdelivered mail and timed noises, and notes that no explanations or paperwork will change their mind.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality and derailment, drifting from their current housing concerns to a past job in logistics and then to a critique of Chicago deep-dish pizza before returning to the original topic.

turns.doctor_question: Over the past few weeks, have you found that you need much less sleep than usual while still feeling full of energy?
turns.patient_response:
Less sleep? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I sleep my usual amount, maybe six or seven hours. I certainly don't feel like I have some boundless supply of energy, just... average, I suppose. 

Though, getting a proper night's rest is highly dependent on your mattress, isn't it? I switched to one of those hybrid memory foam models a few years back. The marketing materials claimed it had "advanced cooling technology," but frankly, the heat retention is a massive design flaw. I actually mapped out the thermal dissipation metrics myself and sent a rather detailed letter to the manufacturer. It’s basic thermodynamics, really. It reminded me of a consulting job I did for a commercial HVAC supplier down in Atlanta back in... oh, it must have been 2004. 

We discovered their main ducting units were losing almost thirty percent efficiency simply due to inadequate joint insulation. Thirty percent! The CEO was absolutely furious when I presented the data. People rarely appreciate the truth when it threatens their profit margins, you know? I had to stand there in this sweltering boardroom—Atlanta in August is completely unbearable, by the way, the humidity just clings to you the moment you step off the plane, it ruins your suits—and explain to these executives that their flagship product was fundamentally flawed. 

...But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, energy. No, my energy levels are completely normal. I sleep fine, assuming the building is quiet.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of sleep to mattresses, thermodynamics, a past consulting job, and Atlanta's humidity before finally returning to the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies having a boundless supply of energy, stating their energy levels are completely normal.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly denies needing less sleep, stating they sleep their usual amount of six or seven hours.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever heard voices or sounds when no one was around that other people couldn't hear?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? Like people talking in my head? No, absolutely not. My mind is perfectly sound. 

I mean, I hear the noises in the walls, like I told you, but those are very real. Anyone standing in my living room would hear them. It's just basic acoustics. Speaking of acoustics, I actually ran a comprehensive cost-variance analysis for a major symphony hall renovation up in Boston... oh, it must have been 2008. The lead architect was absolutely obsessed with using this imported Brazilian cedar for the acoustic baffling. Beautiful wood, certainly, but completely impractical from a budgetary standpoint. I proved to the board of directors that a specialized synthetic composite would yield a fourteen percent improvement in sound diffusion for a third of the price. You have to rely on the metrics, not aesthetics. 

Although, I will say, navigating Boston to get to those board meetings was a complete nightmare. They spent billions on that Big Dig project, supposedly to fix the traffic, but I swear it just moved the gridlock underground. I rented a mid-size sedan at Logan once and spent two hours trapped in a tunnel just trying to get to my hotel near the harbor. The GPS systems back then were practically useless the second you lost line-of-sight with the sky, you know? You'd just be staring at a frozen screen while cars honked at you. 

...Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, voices. No, I don't hear anything like that. Just the actual sounds they make in the building.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of hearing voices to acoustics, a symphony hall renovation, Boston traffic, and GPS systems before losing their train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices or sounds that others cannot hear, stating their mind is perfectly sound.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been feeling persistently down, depressed, or sad lately?
turns.patient_response:
Depressed? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm understandably frustrated by the situation with my apartment, but I'm not sad. I don't sit around crying or feeling down. I'm just trying to deal with the facts of what they're doing to me. 

You know, dealing with facts... that was always the hardest part of my job. People get so emotional when you present them with data that contradicts their worldview. I remember doing a massive workflow optimization for a regional bank out in Denver. This was right around the time they were transitioning to digital record-keeping, maybe 2011? The branch managers were absolutely terrified of the new software. They were convinced it was going to replace them. I had to sit in on these training seminars, and the resistance was just palpable. 

And Denver, well... the altitude really does affect you if you're not used to it. They tell you to drink plenty of water, but nobody mentions how quickly you get winded just walking up a flight of stairs. I stayed at this hotel downtown, right near the 16th Street Mall, and they had this complimentary breakfast buffet. But the eggs... I don't know if it's the boiling point of water at that elevation or what, but the scrambled eggs were always slightly rubbery. I actually calculated the atmospheric pressure differential to see if it correlated with the protein denaturation in the eggs, just out of curiosity. It's fascinating how environmental variables impact simple chemical processes. 

...But no, I'm not depressed. Just... focused on the situation at hand.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, drifting from the topic of depression to a past job in Denver, altitude, and the chemistry of hotel scrambled eggs.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling depressed, sad, or down, stating they do not sit around crying.

turns.patient_response:
Outside of the apartment? Oh, everything else is perfectly fine. When I'm not actively having to document what they're doing to my unit, I manage my finances, I cook all my own meals, I keep all my appointments... I mean, I can still discuss my consulting work or my painting in a completely organized, rational way. 

Speaking of finances, the entire banking sector has really lost its touch when it comes to customer service, haven't they? I was looking at my portfolio last week, just running a standard risk-adjusted return analysis—something I used to do for corporate clients all the time—and I noticed my brokerage firm had changed their fee structure without any clear notification. They buried it in a forty-page PDF! It’s completely unethical. It reminded me of a project I did for a logistics firm in Chicago back in... 2012, I think. 

They were trying to obscure their fuel surcharge increases by bundling them into general administrative fees. I had to build a complete transparency model for their billing department. The CFO was sweating bullets when I showed him the compliance risks. And the winters in Chicago... I don't know how people live there. The wind coming off Lake Michigan literally cuts right through your coat. I bought this supposedly windproof parka before that trip, spent almost four hundred dollars on it, and it was completely useless. The zipper mechanism kept catching on the inner lining. I actually ended up drafting a letter to the manufacturer about the tensile strength of their zipper teeth versus the fabric density. 

...Sorry, what was the question? Oh, my life outside the apartment. Yes, everything else is completely normal and organized. It's just that one specific situation I have to deal with.
